title: Psychological and physiological effects of soundscapes: A systematic review of 25 experiments in the English and Chinese literature

findings.quote: In general, subjective evaluations and objective physiological responses were significantly correlated, particularly within the 1 min of exposure to sound stimuli... This finding demonstrated that the psychological and physiological responses were closely interconnected and equally important in the soundscape research.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to natural sounds (e.g., birdsong, water, ocean waves)
findings.consequent: Positive psychological responses (e.g., pleasantness, arousal, tranquility, preference, visual aesthetic quality, stress reduction, fatigue reduction, annoyance reduction, tension reduction)
findings.quote: Natural sounds enhanced the visual aesthetic quality of distant scenery, farmlands, water views, and roads more than artificial sounds, and they also contributed to a greater sense of tranquility and preference for rural landscapes.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to natural sounds (e.g., birdsong, flowing water, cicada, wind, ocean waves, fountain sounds)
findings.consequent: Positive physiological responses (e.g., reduced HR, RR, RD, SBP, DBP, SCL, increased HRV, AR, alpha/beta EEG, EDA restoration)
findings.quote: Natural sounds reduced HR, RR, and respiratory depth (RD), while increasing the amplitude of the r-wave (AR), HRV, a EEG, and ẞ EEG... natural soundscapes seemed to have a more positive effect on physiological responses than artificial ones.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to artificial sounds (e.g., traffic, construction, machinery, noise, broadcasting, restaurant noise, train noise)
findings.consequent: Negative psychological responses (e.g., less relaxation, hindered restoration, higher attention to traffic, less comfort, less preference, increased tension, fatigue, annoyance)
findings.quote: Artificial sounds were generally evaluated negatively, as traffic sounds and construction sounds were not conducive to relaxation... people generally showed less preference for artificial soundscapes, particularly noise with high decibel levels.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to artificial sounds (e.g., high decibel noise, traffic, street sounds)
findings.consequent: Negative physiological responses (e.g., increased SCL, HR, RR)
findings.quote: High decibel levels of artificial sounds resulted in significantly higher SCL than natural sounds. Traffic sounds and street sounds significantly affected HR and RR.

findings.consequent: Positive psychological responses (e.g., reduced state anxiety, reduced stress, greater restoration benefits, positive emotions)
findings.quote: Audiovisual stimulus had more positive benefits than auditory stimulus alone and significantly reduced state anxiety... Audiovisual stimulus also reduced stress more effectively than visual stimulation alone and provided greater restoration benefits.

findings.antecedent: Audiovisual stimuli (adding sound to visual, or visual to sound)
findings.consequent: Positive physiological responses (e.g., reduced HRV, HF-HRV, ST, RD, HR, alpha EEG; increased LF-HRV, LF/HF-HRV, RR, SCL)
findings.quote: In physiological responses, adding sound to visual stimuli reduced HRV, HF-HRV, skin temperature (ST), and RD, while increasing LF-HRV, LF/HF-HRV, RR, and SCL.

findings.antecedent: Higher soundscape-environment fit/congruence between auditory and visual stimuli
findings.quote: However, the higher the soundscape-environment fit, the higher the preference... a higher level of congruence between soundscapes and environments had more positive psychological responses.

findings.antecedent: Reception of natural elements (e.g., trees, water), spatial patterns (e.g., planting density)
findings.consequent: Enhanced tranquility, reduced state anxiety, positive emotions, reduced stress, increased isolation (for high density), increased excitement (for high density)
findings.quote: In general, the reception of natural elements through visual, auditory, and audiovisual significantly enhanced tranquility. Trees, in particular, contributed more to enhancing tranquility, reducing state anxiety, and promoting positive emotions in both visual and audiovisual experiences, than waterfalls.
